topic: Types of mutation; sickle cell disease
title: The sickle cell variant, from DNA to disease
instructions:
## From one base to a disease

You are the bioinformatics intern at a teaching hospital in Kumasi. A child's beta-globin gene has been sequenced. Compare it with the reference, classify what you see, and advise the family. Examine the evidence before you choose.

nodes.title: The sequence
nodes.text: The lab sends the sixth codon of the HBB gene. Reference: **GAG**. Patient: **GTG**. Look at the genetic code table, then classify the mutation.

evidence.title: Genetic code (extract)
evidence.text:
GAG = glutamic acid (Glu), a charged, hydrophilic amino acid.
GTG = valine (Val), a hydrophobic amino acid.

evidence.title: Aligned reads
evidence.text:
Reference  ...CCT GAG GAG...
Patient    ...CCT GTG GAG...
One base differs at the second position of codon 6: A became T. Nothing inserted or deleted.

choices.feedback: No base was inserted or deleted, so the reading frame is unchanged.
Correct. One base changed and the codon now encodes a different amino acid.
A silent change keeps the same amino acid; GAG to GTG changes Glu to Val.
A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon; GTG is valine.

nodes.title: The protein
nodes.text: Why does one amino acid change make red cells sickle?

choices.text: Valine is hydrophobic, so deoxygenated haemoglobin molecules stick together into fibres that deform the cell
choices.feedback: Correct. The hydrophobic patch lets HbS polymerise when oxygen is low.

choices.text: The protein is no longer made at all
choices.feedback: HbS is made in normal amounts; its behaviour is the problem.

choices.text: The gene is read in a different frame
choices.feedback: The frame is intact; only one amino acid differs.

nodes.title: The family
nodes.text: Both parents are carriers (one HbS allele each) and are well. They ask the chance that their next child has sickle cell disease.

choices.feedback: Half the children would be carriers, but disease needs two HbS alleles.
Correct. Autosomal recessive: AS × AS gives 1 in 4 SS.
Only children who inherit HbS from both parents are affected.

nodes.title: The malaria connection
nodes.text: Why is the HbS allele common in Ghana despite the disease it causes when homozygous?

choices.text: Carriers are partly protected against severe malaria, so selection keeps the allele in the population
choices.feedback: Correct. Heterozygote advantage, a classic case of balancing selection.

choices.text: The mutation happens afresh at a high rate
choices.feedback: Mutation rates are tiny; selection maintains the allele.
SS individuals have serious disease; without a benefit the allele would decline.

nodes.title: The test
nodes.text: The hospital wants a cheap newborn screening test. Which approach fits a district lab?

choices.feedback: Far too costly for one known variant.

choices.text: A targeted assay for the known base change, or haemoglobin electrophoresis
choices.feedback: Correct. A known single-base variant needs a targeted test; electrophoresis separates HbA from HbS by the charge Glu→Val removed.

choices.text: Counting red cells under a microscope
choices.feedback: Sickled cells are visible only in crisis.

nodes.title: Case closed
nodes.text: You classify the variant as the missense substitution c.20A>T (p.Glu6Val), explain the 25% risk, and recommend targeted screening.

hints: Compare the codons base by base.
Glu is charged; Val is hydrophobic.
Draw the Punnett square for AS × AS.

checks.label: You looked at the aligned reads before classifying
At least four of the five decisions are right
checks.message: Fewer than four of the five were right. Read the feedback and run the case again.

realityNote: Ghana's newborn sickle cell screening in Kumasi has run since 1995 using haemoglobin electrophoresis; HBB c.20A>T is in every clinical variant database.
